prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow time to be measured with unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks (B004) to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The reading of round 1 has strengthened my view of why, and the reasons are scientific and not the count. The original idea is separable and identifiable: choose the wavelength at which the light shift of the two clock levels cancels, so that thousands of neutral atoms can be held in a lattice that removes Doppler and recoil effects without perturbing the transition. That is not contained in the frequency comb, which counts optical cycles, and not in single-ion control, which solves the problem with one particle at the price of statistics. The experiment then verified it: first strontium lattice clocks, followed by record systematics and stability at the 1e-18 level, reproduced by independent laboratories on several continents and compared over fibre and satellite links. This is the 'original experiment' that I look for, and it is verified beyond doubt. It also opens a door, as the committee said of attosecond physics in 2023: resolution of gravitational redshift over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and a path to redefine the second. I accept Danielsson's and Lindroth's point that the constants tests are so far null, so I rest the award on the new measurement regime and not on a claimed fundamental discovery. A two-name credit follows the two decisive contributions, the proposal and first realisation, and the accuracy and many-body frontier. My answers to the chair's questions are: yes, distinct from 2005 and 2012 if the citation names the magic-wavelength lattice itself; two names are defensible; and the measured performance suffices without waiting for the redefinition.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains overlap and priority. The comb prize of 2005 and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks were preconditions, and a sceptic can read the lattice clock as an excellent refinement of precision spectroscopy rather than a new discovery. The citation must therefore be worded around the lattice-trapped neutral atoms and not around clocks in general, and I would insist that it not imply a discovery about nature that has not been made. Second, credit for the early record (Lemonde and the SYRTE group, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow, Oates and others) is not captured, and in round 1 nobody showed a specific decisive contribution that requires a third seat. I still cannot settle from memory whether the original-work boundary falls on the theoretical proposal or the first operating clock, but both lie with Katori and the committee's task is to check that against the primary publications before the final citation. Third, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so part of the practical payoff is still prospective, although the physics is not.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the comb counts optical cycles and does not contain the idea of trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, and that the redefinition and null constants tests mean the case should rest on capability.
responses.response: I accept this distinction and I think it answers the chair's first question. The 2005 prize gave the clockwork and the 2012 prize gave control of one ion, but the magic-wavelength lattice is what allows many neutral atoms to be interrogated at once without a light shift, and I would ask that the citation say so. I also agree that we should not lean on the constants tests, which have so far given limits and not a discovery. I would write the citation about invention and realisation and the new accuracy and stability, which is what the record verifies, and leave the foundational uses as consequences.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B010) for its prediction-then-experiment structure and concedes that the pairing mechanism is open, that Yuan Cao is outside the trio and that B004 may be the stronger mature choice if the overlap is settled.
responses.response: I think the overlap question is settled well enough, on the physics, for you to move to B004, and you asked for a view from the experimentalists who can judge it. The idea and its experimental confirmation in independent laboratories are on the record. For B010 I share the high regard for the prediction, but I cannot be absolutely sure of the credited names while the first author of the decisive 2018 devices and the earlier moire band-structure theorists are outside the trio, and the field is eight years old with an unsettled mechanism. I would keep it as the first alternative for a later year, and I would welcome a statement from you whether the Cao problem is solvable within three names, because I do not see how.

responses.point: Kroll values the tidy two-name attribution and raised the possibility of a two-part prize pairing the clock with a quantum-technology topic such as circuit QED, at a cost to credit coherence.
responses.response: I would not add a second part. You yourself identified that the credit coherence of the single-topic prize is its virtue, and no second candidate has a clean attribution: B034 has an unresolved four-to-three name problem and follows the 2025 prize closely, and B036 and B032 have wide and unsettled credit. Adding a part to fill the prize would weaken the strongest element, and I do not regard a count of parts as a measure of the committee's work. On the third seat, I would only add a name if someone can point to a specific decisive publication not covered by Katori and Ye, and none has done so.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks whether a second part such as B032 IceCube or B036 atom interferometry should be added, and notes that the citation must be written around the lattice-clock invention itself.
responses.response: I agree about the citation. On a second part, I agree with your own caution about IceCube: the diffuse flux is established, but the identification of sources is modest, the history involves AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND, and the collaboration is large, so I cannot be sure of the credited people. B036 has a clearer lineage in Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich, but it is a separate precision-measurement prize and it would sit awkwardly beside the clocks. I therefore see no reason for a second part this year and suggest we record B036 and B032 as candidates for a later cycle.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B007 to B004, noting that the clock case is clean but that a refinement-of-an-established-paradigm reading is the main risk, since the conceptual surprise is smaller than for a new phase or a new window on the universe.
responses.response: I share the concern, and I think it is the honest limit of the case. The Physics Prize is for a discovery or an invention, and this is an invention, not a surprise about nature. The way to answer the risk is the citation and the verified record. The invention is separable, it was tested by independent experiment, and it brought a gain of about two orders of magnitude over the caesium standard. I also respect your decision not to defend B007 alone this year when you were the only member who ranked it.

uncertainties: Whether the primary publications place the original contribution on Katori's proposal or on the first strontium lattice clock, and whether the citation should name both the invention and the realisation.
Whether any third name (Lemonde, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow, Oates) can be shown to have a decisive contribution that the two-name credit omits.
Whether the committee as a whole accepts the distinction from the 2005 and 2012 prizes once the citation names the magic-wavelength lattice.
Whether a redefinition of the SI second occurring before the announcement would change the timing argument; I believe it does not change the scientific case.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B004, B010 or B036: my work is in electron microscopy and materials, and I have no documented collaboration with Katori, Ye or the other credited people. I note that Johansson, a Chalmers physics colleague, flagged a possible conflict on B034 and B043, and I support his stepping back from advocating those, which does not affect my preferred configuration. Mehlig is in the neighbouring GU department and Kroll has declared Wallenberg Centre and company ties. None of these is a recusal matter for B004 in my view, and I record no new disclosure since round 1.
